avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP (trauma / stress trigger), seronegative — ICU course

differential.key_features: Trauma history could mask diagnosis; spinal MRI excludes structural lesion.
ICU course raises risk; symmetric ascending pattern with CSF dissociation and demyelinating EMG favours GBS over CIP.
Distinct EMG pattern; CSF dissociation supports GBS.
Electrolytes normal; reflexes preserved in periodic paralysis.

key_clinical_evidence: Trauma and severe stress are recognised triggers for GBS through immune dysregulation.
Seronegativity does not exclude GBS — many cases lack identifiable ganglioside antibodies.
Distinguishing GBS from CIP in ICU patients hinges on time course (GBS precedes ICU course) and CSF dissociation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Symmetric ascending paralysis with CSF dissociation and demyelinating EMG indicates GBS independent of the trauma — trauma is the trigger, not the structural cause.
red_herrings.data_point: Recent head trauma and subarachnoid haemorrhage
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on cervical cord trauma or post-traumatic critical illness rather than GBS.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending quadriplegia and bulbar weakness developing on day 2 of hospitalization for head trauma with subarachnoid hemorrhage.

past_medical_history: Mountain fall 2 days ago — sustained minor trauma, now admitted

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 72-year-old man with vascular dementia who was brought to the emergency department 2 days ago after a mountain fall. He sustained a head injury with multiple bruising. CT head showed subarachnoid hemorrhage and acute subdural hematoma with bilateral parietooccipital hypodensities. He received a tetanus vaccine. His GCS on admission was 13. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated CK at 20,518 IU/L from crush injury. CT angiography showed no aneurysm or vasospasm. His wounds were treated. On hospital day 2 — which is now — he is developing progressive ascending weakness of all four extremities and is noted to have bulbar weakness with reduced gag. He cannot lift his legs and has marked bilateral upper extremity weakness. Global areflexia is present. His SpO2 has dropped to 93% on room air. This acute ascending neurological deterioration in the context of head trauma raised concern for central nervous system injury progression, post-traumatic myelopathy, and other new neurological complications. The bilateral parietooccipital MRI signal changes likely represent posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) in the context of hypertension and trauma — these do not explain the peripheral areflexia and ascending paralysis.

neurological_exam.additional: Admitted 2 days ago for mountain fall — head CT showed subarachnoid hemorrhage and subdural hematoma, bilateral parietooccipital hypodensities. MRI brain on admission showed bilateral T2/FLAIR/DWI hyperintensities in parietooccipital regions. MR angiography: no aneurysm, no stenosis. CK elevated on admission (20,518 IU/L from crush injury). Tetanus vaccine given. IV tazobactam/piperacillin started for skin abrasion wound on day 6. Ascending weakness began on day 2 of hospitalization — AFTER the trauma.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Mild dysarthria — bulbar involvement. Gag reduced bilaterally.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 13 on admission (E3V4M6). Confused, limited historian. Known baseline dementia.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 2 of admission: ascending weakness developing — bilateral lower extremity hip flexion 2/5, knee 2/5, ankle 1/5. Upper extremity: shoulder 3/5, grip 3+/5. Unable to lift legs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Limited assessment by confusion/sedation — appears diminished distally.
